title: Course Delivery and Progress Platform
summary: A teaching platform for a small institution: enrolment, lesson delivery, submissions, and a progress view that three different roles each read for a different reason.
role: Lead engineer, and the person who still maintains it

cover.alt: Placeholder standing in for the course delivery platform cover image.

overview: Three roles use this and none of them want the same thing. A learner wants to know what is due. An instructor wants to know who is stuck. An administrator wants to know whether a cohort is on track. The first version gave all three the same dashboard and none of them used it.

The data model is a three-role permission grid over enrolments, and almost every hard bug in the first year was a permission question wearing a rendering costume. Making the role explicit in the query rather than in the component is what eventually made those bugs boring.
capabilities: Enrols learners into cohorts with a defined start and end
Delivers lessons in a fixed sequence, with prerequisites enforced server side
Accepts submissions as files or text, and keeps every revision
Shows each of the three roles a progress view built for what that role does next
Exports a cohort's progress as a file an administrator can hand to someone else
Keeps an audit trail of every grade change, including who changed it

features.title: One permission model, applied in the query
features.body: Role and cohort scoping are arguments to the data access layer, not conditions inside components. A component that decides what to render based on a role will eventually render the right thing while having fetched the wrong thing.

features.title: Three progress views, not one dashboard
features.body: The learner view answers what is due, the instructor view answers who is stuck, and the administrator view answers whether the cohort is on track. They share a data source and nothing else, because the shared version answered none of the three questions well.

features.title: Submissions keep their history
features.body: Every revision is retained rather than overwritten. Grading disputes are the reason: a submission that can only show its latest state cannot answer what was there when it was marked.

features.title: Sequence rules live on the server
features.body: Prerequisite checks run where the data is. Client-side gating is a hint about what to show, never the thing that decides what a learner can open.

features.title: An audit trail for grades
features.body: Grade changes are append-only and carry the actor. This was not in the first version, and adding it after the first dispute was considerably more work than it would have been on day one.

codeSnippets.title: Scoping at the data layer
codeSnippets.note: The viewer is a required argument, so a caller cannot forget it.

codeSnippets.title: The end-to-end test that guards the three views
codeSnippets.note: One test per role, asserting on what that role should not see as well.

codeSnippets.title: Grade changes are append-only
codeSnippets.code:
CREATE TABLE grade_event (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  submission_id uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES submission (id),
  actor_id      uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES account (id),
  score         numeric(5,2) NOT NULL,
  note          text,
  recorded_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- No UPDATE and no DELETE are granted on this table. The current grade is the most
-- recent event, which is a view, not a column somebody can quietly overwrite.
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON grade_event FROM application;

lessons: A shared dashboard for three roles is usually three unfinished dashboards.
Permission bugs that present as rendering bugs are permission bugs. Fix them where the data is fetched.
An audit trail is cheap to add before the first dispute and expensive afterwards.
Maintaining something for two years teaches more about the first design than shipping it did.

caseStudy.challenge: The first progress view was one dashboard for all three roles, built that way because the underlying data was the same and a single view looked like the economical choice. It was used by nobody. Learners could not find what was due without reading past cohort statistics, instructors could not see who was stuck without filtering, and administrators got a page dense with individual detail they had no use for.
caseStudy.decision: Split it into three views over one query layer, and accept the duplication in the presentation while refusing it in the data access. The alternative considered was a configurable dashboard with per-role defaults, which was rejected because it would have made every future change a question about the configuration system rather than about the view someone was actually looking at.
caseStudy.outcome: All three views are used, and the query layer stayed single. The cost is real: a change to how progress is computed touches three components instead of one, and twice now a fix has landed in two of the three. A shared test that runs the same assertions against all three views is what catches it, and that test exists because it was missed the first time.
